passages.happening:
Ahab tells Jezebel everything Elijah has done, and how he killed the prophets. Jezebel sends a messenger to Elijah with an oath that by the same time tomorrow she will take his life (verses 1-2). ‘And Elijah was afraid and ran for his life’ (verse 3). He comes to Beersheba in Judah, leaves his servant there, and goes on alone a day's walk into the wilderness. ‘He sat down under a broom tree and prayed that he might die’ (verse 4). “I have had enough, LORD,” he says, “Take my life, for I am no better than my fathers” (verse 4).

He lies down under the tree and falls asleep. An angel touches him and says, “Get up and eat” (verse 5). By his head is a cake of bread baked on hot coals and a jar of water. He eats and drinks and lies down again (verse 6). The angel of the LORD comes a second time, touches him, and tells him to eat, for the way ahead is too long for him. ‘So he got up and ate and drank. And strengthened by that food, he walked forty days and forty nights until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 18 ended with fire from heaven, a people on their faces, and rain on the land. Chapter 19 opens with a single threat from Jezebel, and the prophet runs. Carmel proved that the LORD is God, but it did not end Baal's worship in the palace or make Elijah safe.

Jezebel's message uses a standard curse formula, calling on the gods to punish her if she fails. Sending a messenger rather than soldiers may suggest that she wanted Elijah gone rather than made a martyr, though the text does not say.

Beersheba was the traditional southern edge of the land, in Judah and out of Ahab's reach, and Elijah goes a day further into the wilderness of the Negev. The broom tree is a desert shrub that gives a little shade. Elijah leaves his servant behind and goes on alone.

The chapter turns inward, to the prophet's exhaustion and his sense of failure. God's first answer is not a word. It is sleep, a touch, bread and water, more sleep, and a second touch and meal.
passages.later: Moses prayed the same prayer under a heavy load: “If this is how You are going to treat me, please kill me right now” (Numbers 11:15), and God answered him with help, not rebuke. Moses, too, spent ‘forty days and forty nights’ on the mountain of God (Exodus 24:18).
passages.hard:
Elijah asked to die. How does the Bible treat his prayer, and how does God answer him?

Elijah had seen fire fall on Carmel, and one threat sent him running. Exhaustion after great effort, fear of a real danger, and the disappointment of seeing nothing change all appear in the text. His words, that he is no better than his fathers, suggest that he had hoped to be the one who turned Israel back, and now felt that he had failed.

The Bible does not hide his prayer or scold him for it. God's answer is striking in its order: sleep, then food and water, then sleep and food again, before any words at all. Then a question that invites Elijah to speak. Then a quiet presence. And last, work to do, a companion, and the news that he is not the only one left. God treated Elijah's despair as real, and he did not treat it as the last word. He did not leave Elijah by himself with it, and he kept him alive.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: God met a worn-out prophet with sleep and bread before he gave him any words. Ask whether you are caring for your body as part of caring for your soul. And ask who near you might be under a broom tree, and what a meal and a quiet presence could mean to them.

passages.happening:
At Horeb Elijah goes into a cave for the night, and the word of the LORD comes to him: “What are you doing here, Elijah?” (verse 9). He answers, “I have been very zealous for the LORD, the God of Hosts” (verse 10). The Israelites have forsaken God's covenant, torn down his altars and killed his prophets, and ‘I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well’ (verse 10).

The LORD tells him to stand on the mountain, for the LORD is about to pass by. A great wind tears at the mountains and shatters the rocks, ‘but the LORD was not in the wind’ (verse 11). After the wind there is an earthquake, and after the earthquake a fire, and the LORD is in neither. “And after the fire came a still, small voice” (verse 12). When Elijah hears it, he wraps his face in his cloak and stands at the mouth of the cave. The voice asks again, “What are you doing here, Elijah?” (verse 13), and Elijah gives the same answer, word for word (verse 14).

Then the LORD sends him back: to the Desert of Damascus, to anoint Hazael king over Aram, Jehu king over Israel, and Elisha to succeed him as prophet (verses 15-16). And he tells him, ‘Nevertheless, I have reserved seven thousand in Israel’ (verse 18), all whose knees have not bowed to Baal.
passages.hearers:
Horeb is the name Deuteronomy and other books use for Mount Sinai, where God gave Israel the law through Moses. Its exact location is debated, with the traditional site in the southern Sinai peninsula and others proposed in Midian, in northwest Arabia, and elsewhere.

The chapter is full of echoes of Moses. Elijah travels forty days and forty nights, as Moses spent forty days on the mountain. He enters the cave; the Hebrew has the cave, which some readers connect with the cleft of the rock where Moses stood. And the LORD passes by, as he passed before Moses. Fire, smoke and a shaking mountain had marked God's coming at Sinai, yet here the LORD is not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire.

The phrase in verse 12 is in Hebrew a voice, or sound, of thin silence, a deliberately strange expression. Translations vary: a still, small voice, a gentle whisper, a sound of sheer silence. Whatever its exact sense, it stands against the noise before it. It does not teach that God never works in power; Carmel had just shown that he does. It teaches that he is not bound to the dramatic.

Elijah gives the same answer twice, which shows that the vision has not yet changed how he sees himself. He has been zealous, in Hebrew qana, the word used for God's own jealous love for his people, but his zeal has become the lens through which he sees himself as alone. God answers with work and with a correction. Elijah is not the only one left. The word for the seven thousand who are left lies behind the prophets' later idea of the remnant.

Hazael did become king of Aram later in the ninth century, and an Assyrian inscription calls him the son of a nobody, meaning a usurper. Jehu seized Israel's throne about 841 BC and appears on the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III.
passages.later:
Paul quotes this answer to show that God had not rejected his people: “I have reserved for Myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal” (Romans 11:4). In the same way, he says, ‘at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace’ (Romans 11:5).

At Sinai God had told Moses, ‘when My glory passes by, I will put you in a cleft of the rock’ (Exodus 33:22). And Elijah himself appears with Moses beside Jesus on the mountain (Mark 9:4).
passages.asks: Elijah was sure he was the only one left, and he was wrong by seven thousand. Ask where you have decided that you stand alone, and who you may have failed to see. And ask whether you are listening for God only in the wind and the fire, and missing him in the quiet.

passages.t: A cloak thrown over a ploughman
passages.happening:
Elijah finds Elisha son of Shaphat ploughing with twelve teams of oxen; he himself is with the twelfth. ‘Elijah passed by him and threw his cloak around him’ (verse 19). Elisha leaves the oxen, runs after him, and says, “Please let me kiss my father and mother goodbye, and then I will follow you” (verse 20). “Go on back,” Elijah answers, “for what have I done to you?” (verse 20).

Elisha goes back. He slaughters his pair of oxen, cooks the meat on the wood of the yoke and the plough, and gives it to the people to eat. ‘Then he set out to follow and serve Elijah’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Twelve teams of oxen show that Elisha's family was prosperous. Abel-meholah, his home, lay in the Jordan Valley.

A prophet's cloak was part of who he was; Elijah's was probably a hairy garment. Throwing it over Elisha was a sign-act of calling and succession, and the same cloak appears again when Elisha takes it up after Elijah is gone.

Elijah's reply is hard to read. It may mean go, but remember what has been done to you, or simply that the choice is Elisha's own. Elisha's answer is plain. By killing his oxen and burning their gear to cook the meat, he gives up his livelihood and throws a farewell feast, so there is no going back to the farm.

The prophet who thought he was alone now has a companion and a successor.
passages.later: The cloak falls to Elisha when Elijah is taken: ‘Elisha also picked up the cloak that had fallen from Elijah’ (2 Kings 2:13). Another prophet was called from his work in the same way. Amos said, ‘the LORD took me from following the flock’ (Amos 7:15).
passages.asks: Elisha burned his plough so that he could not go back. Ask what you are keeping in reserve in case following God does not work out. And ask whom God has put beside you, as he put Elisha beside Elijah, so that you do not serve alone.
